title: Composition by equivalences on Segal mapping spaces
statement:
Use small simplicial sets, Kan complexes and weak homotopy equivalences from [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], the Kan model structure of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper], and Reedy fibrancy from [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure]. Let $V:\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{sSet}$ be Reedy fibrant with consecutive-edge maps $V_n\to V_1\times_{V_0}\cdots\times_{V_0}V_1$ weak homotopy equivalences for $n\geq2$. For vertices $x,y$, put $M(x,y)=\operatorname{fib}_{(x,y)}((d_1,d_0):V_1\to V_0^2)$, and use the homotopy category $hV$ and invertible components described in [lem-coef-segal-homotopy-category-components]. A simplicial homotopy of maps $u,v:P\to Q$ is a map $P\times\Delta^1\to Q$ with restrictions $u,v$ at the endpoints.

For vertices $x,y,z$ of $V_0$, let $M(x,y,z)$ be the strict fiber of $V_2\to V_0^3$ at $(x,y,z)$. The map $\theta=(d_2,d_0):M(x,y,z)\to M(x,y)\times M(y,z)$ is a trivial Kan fibration and admits a simplicial section $s$. Put $c_{x,y,z}=d_1s$. Its simplicial homotopy class is independent of $s$. These classes are associative and unital: the two composites on $M(x,y)\times M(y,z)\times M(z,w)$ are simplicially homotopic, and the maps $g\mapsto c_{x,x,y}(s_0x,g)$ and $f\mapsto c_{x,y,y}(f,s_0y)$ on $M(x,y)$ are each simplicially homotopic to its identity. On components $c$ induces composition in $hV$. For every section $s$, one has $d_1\simeq c_{x,y,z}\theta$ on $M(x,y,z)$.

If $f\in M(x,y)_0$ represents an isomorphism in $hV$, then the maps
$$f^*:M(y,z)\longrightarrow M(x,z),\quad g\longmapsto c_{x,y,z}(f,g),\qquad f_*:M(w,x)\longrightarrow M(w,y),\quad h\longmapsto c_{w,x,y}(h,f)$$
are weak homotopy equivalences for every $z,w$. Their maps on components are respectively precomposition and postcomposition by $[f]$, so both preserve and reflect invertible components.

proof.text: Use the mapping simplicial sets, discrete representables $F(n)$, and constant simplicial spaces $cK$ of [lem-coef-simplicial-space-reedy-cartesian]. Let $G(n)\subseteq F(n)$ be the union of consecutive edges and let $D(n)\subseteq G(n)$ be the union of its $n+1$ vertices. Evaluation on the identity of $[n]$ identifies $\operatorname{Map}(F(n),V)=V_n$: a simplex $v$ determines the map whose value on $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$ is $V(\alpha)v$. Mapping out of the edge union identifies $\operatorname{Map}(G(n),V)$ with the composable-edge product, since maps on the edges agree precisely at common vertices; likewise $\operatorname{Map}(D(n),V)=V_0^{n+1}$. These are isomorphisms of simplicial sets commuting with restriction. For a fixed list $\mathbf{x}=(x_0,\ldots,x_n)$, write $T_n(\mathbf{x})$ for the strict fiber of $V_n\to V_0^{n+1}$ and $P_n(\mathbf{x})=\prod_{i=1}^n M(x_{i-1},x_i)$. The fiber of spine restriction is therefore the actual map $\theta_n:T_n(\mathbf{x})\to P_n(\mathbf{x})$.

source.place: Section 5.1, mapping fibers and the displayed fiberwise Segal comparison; explicit evaluation at the identity simplex

proof.text: All inclusions of the finite discrete shapes just defined are monomorphisms. The mapping assertion of [lem-coef-simplicial-space-reedy-cartesian], applied to the Reedy fibration $V\to *$, makes each restriction a Kan fibration, and the mapping complex of each shape is Kan by taking the inclusion of the empty shape. In particular $V_1\to V_0^2$ is a Kan fibration, so every $M(x,y)$ is Kan: lift a horn after pairing its fixed endpoint coordinates. The unrestricted spine restriction is a Kan fibration and is a weak equivalence by the Segal hypothesis. It is thus a trivial Kan fibration in [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. Fixing vertices is a pullback of that trivial fibration: $T_n=V_n\times_{\operatorname{Map}(G(n),V)}P_n$. Any boundary lifting problem for this pullback projects to one for the unrestricted restriction, whose filler pairs with the prescribed $P_n$ coordinate. The boundary characterization of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper] proves that every $\theta_n$, $n\geq2$, is a trivial Kan fibration. The same pullback horn-lifting argument shows that restricting between any of our finite shapes while fixing all their vertices is a Kan fibration.

source.place: Sections 2.4-2.5 and 5.1: unrestricted and fiberwise restriction fibrations; explicit pullback lifting

proof.text: A trivial Kan fibration $p:E\to B$ lifts against every monomorphism: [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper] states boundary lifting and that every monomorphism is a transfinite composite of pushouts of coproducts of boundaries, so extend a lift successively across these cells and glue at limits. In particular lifting against $\varnothing\to B$ gives a section. More generally, if $a,b:K\to E$ satisfy $pa=pb=r$, lift the endpoint map $(a,b):K\times\partial\Delta^1\to E$ over $r\operatorname{pr}_K:K\times\Delta^1\to B$. Its left map is degreewise injective, so the filler is a simplicial homotopy $a\simeq b$ over $B$. Apply this first with $p=\theta_2$ to two sections: postcomposition by $d_1$ proves section independence of $c=d_1s$. Apply it again with $K=T_2$, $a=1_{T_2}$, $b=s\theta_2$, and $r=\theta_2$; postcomposition by $d_1$ gives $d_1\simeq c\theta_2$ for every section, as required.

source.place: Sections 5.1-5.3; explicit boundary-cylinder lift comparing choices (also the lifting argument of Stacks Tag 08NS, lemma-trivial-kan-homotopy)

proof.text: We will combine homotopies only with Kan targets. By [lem-cbc-kan-functor-space-kan], if $Q$ is Kan then $\operatorname{Fun}(K,Q)$ is Kan for every simplicial set $K$. By the internal-functor definition of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], an edge of this complex is exactly a map $K\times\Delta^1\to Q$, with its two vertex maps as endpoints. Two consecutive edges combine to one edge by filling $\Lambda_1^2$; an edge $u\to v$ can be reversed by filling the horn with edges $u\to v$ and the degenerate edge $u\to u$, obtaining $v\to u$. Thus any finite chain of simplicial homotopies into $Q$ is a single simplicial homotopy. The same argument for $K=\Delta^0$ converts any finite zigzag of edges in a Kan complex into a path of either desired orientation. Components are detected by such zigzags: all vertices of each simplex are linked by edges, while the union of simplices in any one vertex-edge equivalence class and its complement have closed preimages in every simplex of the realization. They give disjoint open-and-closed pieces of the realization, and each piece is path connected via its simplices and edge paths. Consequently equal mapping components give the vertex paths used below.

source.place: Section 5.3: components and homotopies; explicit Kan horn compression of paths and mapping-space homotopies

proof.text: Fix $x,y,z,w$ and put $P=M(x,y)\times M(y,z)\times M(z,w)$, with coordinates $(a,b,h)$. Inside $F(3)$ let $A$ be the union of triangles $012$ and $023$ along their common edge $02$, and let $B$ be the union of triangles $123$ and $013$ along $13$. Their fixed-vertex mapping spaces $A_V,B_V$ are strict spaces of pairs of triangles agreeing on the common edge. Projection $A_V\to T_2(x,y,z)\times M(z,w)$ forgets triangle $023$ except for its prescribed edges $02,23$; it is the pullback of $\theta_2$ for $(x,z,w)$ along $(t,h)\mapsto(d_1t,h)$. Projection from that target to $P$ is $\theta_2\times1$, itself a pullback of a trivial fibration. Hence $A_V\to P$ is trivial by successive boundary lifts. For $B_V$, first forget triangle $013$ except for its prescribed edges $01,13$, giving the pullback of $\theta_2$ for $(x,y,w)$ over $M(x,y)\times T_2(y,z,w)$; the subsequent projection is $1\times\theta_2$. Thus $B_V\to P$ is also trivial. Restriction $r_A:T_3(x,y,z,w)\to A_V$ is a Kan fibration by step 2 and satisfies $(A_V\to P)r_A=\theta_3$. Both maps to $P$ are weak equivalences; two-out-of-three from the model-category axioms in [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure] makes $r_A$ a weak equivalence, hence a trivial Kan fibration. The identical argument applies to $r_B$. The chosen sections define a map $P\to A_V$ by the triangles $s_{x,y,z}(a,b)$ and $s_{x,z,w}(c(a,b),h)$, which agree exactly on $02$. Lifting it through $r_A$ yields $u_A:P\to T_3$. Similarly the triangles $s_{y,z,w}(b,h)$ and $s_{x,y,w}(a,c(b,h))$ lift through $r_B$ to $u_B$. Both are sections of $\theta_3$. Step 3 supplies a homotopy $u_A\simeq u_B$; evaluating the long edge $03$ gives $c(c(a,b),h)\simeq c(a,c(b,h))$. Indeed $03$ is the long edge of triangle $023$ on $u_A$ and of $013$ on $u_B$; these are the same edge restriction of $F(3)$ (equivalently $d_1d_1=d_1d_2$). This proves associativity as a homotopy of maps on the entire product $P$, for arbitrary choices of the sections.

source.place: Proposition 5.4 and Proposition 11.3: explicit parameterized two-triangle gluing and comparison, expanding the source diagrams

proof.text: For $K=M(x,y)$ the maps $K\to T_2(x,x,y)$ given by $s_{x,x,y}(s_0x,-)$ and the degeneracy $s_0:K\to T_2(x,x,y)$ have the same $\theta_2$ projection $(s_0x,-)$. Step 3 compares them by a simplicial homotopy; applying $d_1$ and $d_1s_0=1$ proves $c(s_0x,-)\simeq1_K$. For the other unit, compare $s_{x,y,y}(-,s_0y)$ and $s_1:K\to T_2(x,y,y)$ over $(-,s_0y)$ and use $d_1s_1=1$. By [lem-coef-segal-homotopy-category-components], the chosen triangle $s(a,b)$ computes precisely the composition $[b]\circ[a]$ in $hV$, and its degenerate arrows compute identities. Thus the maps just constructed have the asserted componentwise interpretation, and their associative and unital homotopies realize the corresponding laws of $hV$.

source.place: Proposition 5.4, degeneracy proof of the unit laws, and Section 5.5, the homotopy category

proof.text: Let $f:x\to y$ represent an isomorphism in $hV$. By [lem-coef-segal-homotopy-category-components], the inverse morphism is represented by a vertex $g\in M(y,x)$ and satisfies $[c(f,g)]=[s_0x]$ and $[c(g,f)]=[s_0y]$; recall the order $c(a,b)=b\circ a$. Steps 2 and 4 give vertex paths $\alpha:\Delta^1\to M(x,x)$ from $c(f,g)$ to $s_0x$ and $\beta:\Delta^1\to M(y,y)$ from $c(g,f)$ to $s_0y$. For each $z$ define $F:M(y,z)\to M(x,z)$ by $F(k)=c(f,k)$ and $G:M(x,z)\to M(y,z)$ by $G(l)=c(g,l)$. Associativity from step 5, restricted along the fixed vertices $g,f$, gives $GF(k)=c(g,c(f,k))\simeq c(c(g,f),k)$. The actual map $(k,t)\mapsto c(\beta(t),k)$ homotopes the latter to $c(s_0y,k)$, and step 6 homotopes it to $k$. Likewise $FG(l)=c(f,c(g,l))\simeq c(c(f,g),l)\simeq c(s_0x,l)\simeq l$, using the map $(l,t)\mapsto c(\alpha(t),l)$. Step 4 compresses each chain to a single simplicial homotopy, since its target mapping space is Kan. Therefore $G$ is a simplicial homotopy inverse to $F=f^*$.

source.place: Sections 5.5 and 11.2, Proposition 11.3 and Corollary 11.5: explicit inverse equations and precomposition homotopies

proof.text: For each $w$ define $U:M(w,x)\to M(w,y)$ by $U(k)=c(k,f)$ and $R:M(w,y)\to M(w,x)$ by $R(l)=c(l,g)$. The associativity homotopy restricts to $RU(k)=c(c(k,f),g)\simeq c(k,c(f,g))$. The map $(k,t)\mapsto c(k,\alpha(t))$ then gives $c(k,c(f,g))\simeq c(k,s_0x)$, and the right unit homotopy gives $k$. Similarly $UR(l)=c(c(l,g),f)\simeq c(l,c(g,f))\simeq c(l,s_0y)\simeq l$, using $(l,t)\mapsto c(l,\beta(t))$ and the right unit at $y$. Compress the two chains by step 4. This constructs a simplicial homotopy inverse $R$ for $U=f_*$.

source.place: Section 11.2, Proposition 11.3 and Corollary 11.5: explicit postcomposition inverse homotopies

proof.text: Apply [lem-cbc-simplicial-homotopy-equivalence-weak] to $(F,G)$ and $(U,R)$ with their two endpoint homotopies from steps 7 and 8. It implies that $f^*$ and $f_*$ are weak homotopy equivalences. Step 6 identifies their component functions with $[k]\mapsto[k]\circ[f]$ and $[k]\mapsto[f]\circ[k]$. Multiplying an isomorphism by $[f]$ gives an isomorphism. Conversely, if $[k]\circ[f]$ is invertible, then $[k]=([k]\circ[f])\circ[g]$ is invertible; if $[f]\circ[k]$ is invertible, then $[k]=[g]\circ([f]\circ[k])$ is invertible. This proves preservation and reflection of the invertible components. The constructions work for empty mapping complexes: all lifting assertions include dimension zero and a map out of the empty complex is unique; an assumed inverse class already supplies a representative when needed. No completeness or connectedness assumption has entered.

source.place: Corollary 11.5, plus the explicit componentwise inverse calculation
